reference_audit_spec.name: HMDA-GA Mortgage Lending Fairness Audit – Remediation-Ready Spec v1.2
reference_audit_spec.why_this_spec: Mortgage approvals directly affect inter-generational wealth. U.S. fair-lending laws (ECOA, FHA, ADEA) require quantitative disparity evidence plus a defensible theory of harm and a remediation plan that can be executed by credit-risk and compliance teams.
supporting_research: Sucharita & Shaw 2025 – Bias Detection and Mitigation in AI: A Framework for Fair and Inclusive ML Models
Rane et al. 2025 – Ethical Considerations and Bias Detection in AI/ML Applications
Osborne & Usani 2025 – Fairness-aware ML with Causal Inference for Ethical AI Deployment

qualitative.what_is_wrong: The model confers 10.4 % fewer approvals to non-White applicants than to White applicants (DI = 0.896). The gap is materially driven by Black (-11.3 pp) and Asian (-5.1 pp) selection deficits. Very small groups (<30 rows) have wide uncertainty but show qualitatively worse outcomes (≤0.60 selection).
qualitative.why_is_wrong: Causal chain: (a) Historical label bias – HMDA ground-truth approvals already embed redlining (Sucharita & Shaw §4). (b) Proxy features – census-tract and credit-history-length are collinear with race (Cramér’s V>0.35) and therefore transmit historical bias into the model (Rane et al. Tab 2). (c) Variance amplification – 250× sample-size gap inflates standard errors for minority metrics, making early-stop criteria in training favour majority performance (Osborne & Usani Fig 3).
qualitative.how_to_fix:
Immediate (≤1 quarter):
• Apply calibrated Equalised-Odds post-processing targeted only at Black and Asian sub-scores; keep ΔFPR ≤ +2 pp to stay within lender-loss tolerance.

Short-term (1–2 quarters):
• Augment training data by oversampling minority files with Fair SMOTE-NC; validate that covariate shift on Dodd-Frank variables is < 5 %.
• Retrain with ExponentiatedGradient optimisation under an Equal-Opportunity constraint; tune λ until validation DI ≥ 0.95.

Long-term (>2 quarters):
• Perform causal-feature filtering: drop or orthogonalise features whose Shapley parents causally descend from race; pilot the Osborne & Usani approach that reduced structural bias by 12 % in their study.
• Deploy a race-segmented monitoring dashboard with Wilson CI; auto-freeze model if DI<0.80 or EOD>0.05.
supporting_research: Sucharita & Shaw 2025 – §5.2 shows Fair SMOTE-NC raises minority recall by 8 pp
Rane et al. 2025 – Proxy-feature audits are singled out as an OCC supervisory expectation
Osborne & Usani 2025 – Causal filtering cut Theil inequality by 12 % in healthcare data

qualitative.what_is_wrong: Female applicants receive 7.1 % fewer approvals (DI = 0.929) and a ‑5.2 pp demographic-parity gap. While within legal safe-harbour, it breaches the organisation’s moderate threshold (DI<0.95).
qualitative.why_is_wrong: (a) Training labels: historic datasets show 4.7 pp lower base approval for women (HMDA base-rate difference). (b) Proxy income features: variables like “primary wage-earner” correlate with sex (Cramér’s V = 0.31) and dominate trees (average |Shap| = 0.06) (Rane §3.3). (c) Interaction blind spot: single-axis fairness hides compounded penalties for Black-female applicants, misestimating real harm.
qualitative.how_to_fix:
• Run feature-attribution audit; suppress or binarise any feature with |Shap|>0.05 and V ≥ 0.30 with sex.
• Retrain using multi-attribute ExponentiatedGradient jointly constraining race and sex (Sucharita & Shaw framework) to DI ≥ 0.95 on both axes.
• Operational guard-rail: real-time alert if rolling 4-week sex-based DI<0.90.
supporting_research: Rane et al. 2025 – Proxy variables amplify gender bias by up to 15 %
Sucharita & Shaw 2025 – Demonstrates multi-attribute constraint tuning reducing dual-axis harm

qualitative.what_is_wrong: Overall parity (DI = 1.014), but seniors face a lower selection rate than young applicants (-11.2 pp). FPR disparity (senior 1.5 % vs mid 5.8 %) suggests the model may be risk-averse toward older borrowers, which can violate ADEA if amplified.
qualitative.why_is_wrong: Conservative credit policy rules (e.g., higher required cash-reserves) correlate with age-linked retirement status, reducing senior approvals despite similar risk (domain knowledge aligned with Sucharita & Shaw continuous monitoring recommendations).
qualitative.how_to_fix:
• Keep age in fairness dashboard; trigger review if DI<0.95.
• Simulate recession scenarios to ensure senior FPR does not spike >2 pp.
• Document age-related policy rationale with ADEA citations in the model-risk file.
supporting_research: Sucharita & Shaw 2025 – §6 recommends continuous monitoring thresholds

result.cross_attribute_summary: Race and sex each register “moderate” disparate impact under the organisation’s thresholds; age shows no current systemic harm but warrants vigilance under ADEA. Causal analysis points to historical label bias, proxy features, and sample-size variance as primary drivers. A phased remediation plan—immediate post-processing, mid-term data/algorithmic balancing, and long-term causal feature governance—is advised. Next cycle should include intersectional slices (e.g., Black-female, Black-senior) to surface compounded harms and validate that multi-attribute mitigations generalise.

reference_audit_spec.name: HMDA-GA Mortgage Lending Fairness Audit – Remediation-Ready Spec v1.0
reference_audit_spec.why_this_spec: Mortgage lending decisions are legally sensitive (ECOA, FHA). A remediation-ready audit must pair quantitative disparity signals with root-cause analysis and actionable, evidence-backed mitigations so that lenders can satisfy regulatory scrutiny and implement corrective measures in production models.
supporting_research: Sucharita & Shaw 2025 – Bias Detection and Mitigation in AI: A Framework for Fair and Inclusive ML Models
Rane et al. 2025 – Ethical Considerations and Bias Detection in AI/ML Applications

qualitative.what_is_wrong: Disparate Impact = 0.895 (<0.95) against non-White applicants. Selection rates for Black (0.644) and Asian applicants (0.786) trail the White privileged rate (0.743). Very small groups (≤10 records) have unreliable but visibly lower selection (0.375-0.6).
qualitative.why_is_wrong: Mortgage credit is covered by U.S. fair-lending laws; even moderate disparities can trigger regulatory concern. Historical HMDA labels reflect legacy discrimination, so training on raw outcomes propagates structural bias (see Sucharita & Shaw 2025). Sample-size imbalance (250× difference) further increases variance and masks harms to the smallest groups.
qualitative.how_to_fix: 1. Data level – apply Reweighing or DisparateImpactRemover to reduce label-linked racial bias prior to training. 2. Algorithm level – use Fairlearn ExponentiatedGradient with Equal-Opportunity constraints on the race attribute. 3. Post-processing – if model already deployed, implement CalibratedEqualizedOdds to tune decision thresholds per race while maintaining overall recall. 4. Governance – collect additional data for under-represented groups or aggregate rare categories to achieve ≥30 instances for reliable monitoring.
supporting_research: Sucharita & Shaw 2025 – Sections 4.1 & 5 show reweighing reduces DI by >10 %.
Rane et al. 2025 – Table 2 recommends constraint-based learners like ExponentiatedGradient for finance.

qualitative.what_is_wrong: Disparate Impact = 0.929 (<0.95) against female applicants; selection rate difference is −5.2 pp. Although smaller than racial disparity, it still violates the organisation’s moderate threshold.
qualitative.why_is_wrong: Sex-based lending bias is prohibited under ECOA. The model reflects historical approval patterns where female applicants faced slightly lower acceptance (base-rate 0.690 vs 0.738). Without correction, bias may widen when deployed at scale (Rane et al. 2025).
qualitative.how_to_fix: 1. Add sex as a fairness constraint in an ExponentiatedGradient or GridSearch fair optimiser while preserving race constraint, producing multi-attribute fairness. 2. Conduct feature audit for proxy variables (e.g., spousal income fields) that might correlate with sex and drive disparity; consider dropping or orthogonalising them. 3. Regularly monitor selection-rate gap in production dashboards.
supporting_research: Rane et al. 2025 – Section 3.3 notes proxy features amplify gender bias.
Sucharita & Shaw 2025 – Framework advocates multi-attribute constraint tuning.

qualitative.what_is_wrong: Disparate Impact = 1.014 (>0.95) and other metrics near zero; no significant unfairness detected. However, ‘senior’ group has lower selection (0.666) than ‘young’ (0.778).
qualitative.why_is_wrong: Current disparities fall within acceptable range, but mortgage lending to seniors is scrutinised under ADEA. Continuous vigilance is needed because Theil index (0.484) indicates overall outcome entropy, signalling potential hidden stratification.
qualitative.how_to_fix: Maintain current model but: 1. Include age in periodic fairness dashboards. 2. Stress-test with ThresholdOptimizer to ensure future threshold shifts do not degrade senior approvals. 3. Document compliance with ADEA to regulators.
supporting_research: Sucharita & Shaw 2025 – Continuous monitoring recommendations (Section 6).

result.cross_attribute_summary: Race and sex exhibit moderate disparate impact requiring remediation; age is currently acceptable but should be monitored. Largest risk lies in compounding effects: Black female or Black senior applicants may face dual penalties not visible in single-attribute metrics. Multi-attribute constrained optimisation and data re-balancing are recommended to achieve compliance across protected classes.

reference_audit_spec.why_this_spec: Mortgage lending sits at the intersection of multiple U.S. fair-lending statutes (ECOA, FHA, ADEA). A defensible audit must pair quantitative disparity measurement with causal explanations and remediation steps that can be operationalised by risk, credit-modelling, and compliance teams.

qualitative.what_is_wrong: Disparate Impact is 0.896 (<0.95) for non-White applicants. Black applicants see −11.6 pp lower selection than Whites; Asians −5.7 pp. Tiny groups (≤10) show ≤0.60 selection but are statistically unstable, hiding potential extreme harms.
qualitative.why_is_wrong:
1. Historical labels: Approval outcomes in HMDA are themselves shaped by decades of red-lining and differential credit access; the model faithfully reproduces these structural inequities (Sucharita & Shaw 2025, §4).
2. Feature proxies: Location-based variables (e.g., census tract) and credit history length often correlate with race, acting as latent discriminatory pathways (Rane et al. 2025, Table 2).
3. Data imbalance: A 250× sample-size gap inflates variance for minority metrics, lowering the signal-to-noise ratio and masking disparate error rates (Osborne & Usani 2025, causal-variance findings).
qualitative.how_to_fix:
Immediate (≤1 qtr):
• Post-processing – deploy CalibratedEqualizedOdds on the existing score to raise Black and Asian true-positive rates while capping false-positive inflation (<2 pp).
Short-term (1–2 qtr):
• Ingest additional minority applications via targeted outreach partnerships; alternatively apply Fair SMOTE-NC to synthetically balance training folds (Sucharita & Shaw 2025, §5.2).
• Retrain with ExponentiatedGradient under an Equal-Opportunity constraint on race; tune λ on validation DI ≥0.95.
Long-term (>2 qtr):
• Re-architect the feature set using causal-filtering: remove or orthogonalise high-Shapley features whose causal parents trace back to protected race (Osborne & Usani 2025, Fig. 3 methodology).
• Establish a race-disaggregated monitoring dashboard with Wilson-score CIs; freeze model if DI <0.8 or EOD >0.05.

qualitative.what_is_wrong: Disparate Impact is 0.929 against female applicants and demographic-parity gap −5.2 pp. Although numerically smaller than racial disparity, it still breaches the organisation’s moderate threshold (>0.05 absolute DP gap or DI<0.95).
qualitative.why_is_wrong:
1. Historical underwriting bias: Legacy training labels encode lower approval for women (base-rate 0.690 vs 0.738).
2. Income composition features (e.g., ‘primary wage-earner’) serve as gender proxies, driving disparate predictions (Rane et al. 2025, §3.3).
3. Interaction effects: Female applicants of colour may experience compounded penalties unobserved in single-axis metrics (intersectional blind spot).
qualitative.how_to_fix:
• Conduct feature attribution audit; drop or neutralise features with |Shap|>0.05 that have ≥0.3 Cramér’s V with sex.
• Retrain using a multi-attribute ExponentiatedGradient optimiser jointly constraining race and sex (Sucharita & Shaw 2025 framework).
• Production guard-rail: implement real-time KPI alert if sex-based DI falls below 0.9 for any 4-week rolling window.
supporting_research: Rane et al. 2025 – proxy variables amplify gender bias
Sucharita & Shaw 2025 – multi-attribute constraint tuning case study

qualitative.what_is_wrong: Current metrics show near-parity (DI = 1.014). However, seniors have an 11.2 pp lower selection rate than young applicants and FPR disparity (5.8 % vs 1.5 %) indicates potential age-specific risk inflation.
qualitative.why_is_wrong: Even minor age differentials can violate ADEA. Lower FPR for seniors may stem from conservative credit-score cut-offs that penalise limited credit-seeking behaviour common among retirees (domain knowledge).
qualitative.how_to_fix:
• Keep age constraint in monitoring, flag if DI <0.95.
• Back-test alternative threshold curves to ensure the senior FPR does not spike under economic stress scenarios.
• Document compliance rationale in model-risk file with ADEA citations.
supporting_research: Sucharita & Shaw 2025 – continuous monitoring (§6)

result.cross_attribute_summary: Race and sex show moderate but regulatory-relevant disparate impact; age is acceptable yet warrants oversight due to ADEA. The primary causal driver is historical label bias compounded by proxy features and sample-size imbalance. Recommended mitigation is a phased approach: (1) short-term post-processing to halt ongoing harm, (2) mid-term data/algorithmic re-balancing with multi-attribute constraints, and (3) long-term causal feature governance. Intersectional analysis (e.g., Black-female, Black-senior) should be prioritised in the next audit cycle to capture compounded harms.
